1.pericope_label: The judgments begin: the Hebrew manservant

schools.summary: Gill explains that these judicial laws touch the civil state of Israel and are called judgments because founded in justice and equity and because the commonwealth was to be governed by them, reports the rabbinic tradition that the man in view was sold by the court for theft records the reading of the phrase for the single man as meaning with his garment while preferring the plain sense of alone, and takes the judges for civil magistrates though the Hebrew says simply to God. Calvin holds that God would have the children of Abraham differ from heathen and ordinary slaves and enjoined their release, but refuses to soften the exception, which shows how hard the slave's condition was since it could not be mitigated without a provision he calls unnatural, nothing being more opposed to nature than so dividing a family.

Henry notes that the government was purely a theocracy, so that what other states settle by human prudence was here settled by divine appointment, and that Moses is now given general statutes in place of particular enquiries. He thinks it deliberate that the code opens with servants, since Israel had lately been servants themselves, and presses that a man who was once abused has no excuse but rather an aggravation if he abuses those under him. In the boring of the ear he finds the servants taught a noble love of liberty as the Lord's freemen, with a mark of disgrace on the man who refused it, and the masters taught not to trample on those who had lately been their equals; and he turns the law upon Christ, whose opened ear in the psalm seems to allude to it, since he would not go out free from his undertaking.

Clarke draws from Calmet six ways in which a Hebrew might lose his liberty, explains the retention of the wife and children by a rule that children born to a Hebrew of a Canaanitish woman counted as Canaanites, prefers the reading that the freed man should have the same coat going out as coming in and quotes Jerome for it, notes that the Hebrew says to God where the Greek gives the judgment of God, and takes the bored ear to signify that the man was bound to hear and obey his master, adding that the custom was an ancient eastern one noticed by the satirists. Wesley allows both self-sale through poverty and sale by the judges for crime, and stresses that even the latter served seven years at most.

Ellicott canvasses the renderings of the title and thinks only the paraphrase gives the full sense, sets the law against a society founded on slavery in which the rights of the slave class come first because likeliest to be infringed, lists crime, debt and a father's right of sale as the roads into servitude, observes that affection grows up under every system of slavery toward an indulgent master as Roman practice showed, notes that the mildness of the Hebrew form would make refusals of freedom common, stresses that a formal act was needed because the State had to sanction a citizen's passing into slavery, and explains that the opening of the ear became a byword for perpetual service. Keil and Delitzsch state the rule of release after six years without compensation, extend it from Deuteronomy to the maidservant, limit it by the word Hebrew to Israelites rather than foreign slaves, and set out the three cases of the man who came single, the man who brought a wife and the man whose master gave him one.

debates: How the exception about the wife and children should be judged. Calvin calls it unnatural and takes it as evidence how hard the slave's condition was; Clarke explains it by the rule that children of a Canaanitish mother counted as Canaanites; Keil and Delitzsch state it without comment as one of three cases.

What the phrase describing the single man means. Gill reports the rendering with his garment but prefers alone; Clarke prefers the former and cites Jerome, arguing that the old coat must have worn out in service.

Who the judges were. Gill and Clarke both note that the Hebrew says simply to God and the Greek the judgment of God, and both understand the magistrates; Ellicott makes the point institutional, that the State had to sanction the change of status.
outliers: Ellicott's observation that Roman slaves would endure the severest torture rather than accuse an indulgent owner.
Henry's argument that a man who was himself once oppressed has no excuse but rather an aggravation if he oppresses those under him.
Clarke's note that the boring of the ear was an ancient eastern custom noticed by the satirists.
themes: laws given instead of case-by-case enquiry
a code that begins with servants
freedom bought at the price of a family
an ear fastened to the door-post

7.pericope_label: The maidservant sold by her father

schools.summary: Gill takes the daughter for a child under twelve put out to service through her father's poverty, renders the clause about the master's dislike as her being evil in his eyes, and rejects the common reading of the three things, making them instead the three dispositions open to the master — to espouse her himself, to betroth her to his son, or to let her be redeemed. Calvin refuses to defend the arrangement, holding that it shows how many vices were of necessity tolerated in this people, that a father's selling his children to relieve poverty was an act of barbarism which could not be corrected as one might have hoped, and that the sanctity of the marriage vow should have counted for more than a liberty to repudiate a betrothed bondmaid or to void a covenant made for a son, since what God has joined man is not to put asunder.

Clarke reports the rabbinic limits — the sale permitted only in extreme distress, when nothing was left even to the clothes on the father's back, and only while the girl was unmarriageable — and compares the servitude to an apprenticeship of seven years, holds that a son marrying his father's servant obliged the father to treat her as a daughter with a daughter's dowry, notes that no abatement was allowed in the first wife's food, raiment or conjugal right when another was taken, identifies that right with the apostle's marriage debt, and counts the three things as flesh rather than a slave's vegetables, raiment, and a due proportion of the husband's company. Wesley reads the betrothal as being to a secondary wife while adding that masters did not always take maidservants on those terms, and says the son's wife must have a portion as to a daughter.

Ellicott frames the sale by the father's power, exercised freely among many ancient nations though comparatively rare in Israel and arising from extreme poverty, notes that such a woman might claim freedom after six years or, if bought to be a wife, keep a wife's status for life even if her husband took another, prefers the reading who hath not betrothed her and explains the remedy as providing a Hebrew substitute to carry out the contract, would render the disputed right more exactly as the right of cohabitation, says plainly that polygamy is treated as lawful here as generally in a law which did not venture to forbid what it discouraged, and states the third of the three alternatives as transferring her on the same terms to another Hebrew. Keil and Delitzsch carry the sequence through from betrothal and redemption to the three things not to be diminished and the release without money if they are withheld.

debates: What the three things are. Clarke counts food, raiment and conjugal right; Gill reports that reading but follows the rabbinic authorities in making them the three dispositions open to the master; Ellicott agrees with Gill and specifies the third as transfer to another Hebrew.

How the clause about the master's dislike should be read. Gill keeps the received sense of her being displeasing to him; Ellicott prefers the variant which makes it that he had not betrothed her, so that the offence is a refusal to complete the contract.

Whether the institution can be defended. Clarke softens it by limits of practice and a comparison with apprenticeship; Ellicott explains it historically by the father's power; Calvin refuses both and calls the father's sale an act of barbarism which the law tolerated without correcting.
outliers: Clarke's comparison of the six years' servitude with an ordinary apprenticeship of seven, the master paying so much a week.
Ellicott's admission that polygamy is treated as lawful here, the legislator allowing much for the hardness of men's hearts.
Clarke's gloss that the woman's food meant flesh, since she was not to be fed like a common slave on vegetables only.
themes: a daughter sold in extremity
betrothed, or not betrothed
the protections of a wife
three things, or three choices

12.pericope_label: Murder, manslaughter, and the capital crimes

schools.summary: Gill refuses to narrow the law of homicide to any nation or instrument, covering any person smitten with anything whatever so that death follows, and lists those the murder law does not reach — the officer of the court, the executioner, the physician, the father or master chastising — since such men act wilfully but not with guile, their design being good; on smiting a parent he notes that death need not follow, a wound or visible mark sufficing, and on manstealing that though the law was given to Israel it was framed for man-stealers generally, as the apostle's use of it shows. Calvin holds that what is commonly called accidental homicide happens not by chance but according to the will of God, as if He led the man who is killed out to his death, takes presumption and guile as two ways of saying one thing since all cruelty is presumptuous, reads the tearing of a murderer from the altar as signifying that he is as unworthy of divine aid as of human, and observes that the capital sanction on smiting a parent shows the rights of parents sacred, God going further than the Roman law which drowned the parricide in a sack.

Henry sets the law beside the commandment lately given and argues that God, who by his providence gives and maintains life, here by his law protects it, so that mercy shown to a wilful murderer is real cruelty to all mankind besides; he allows no distinction between sudden passion and malice prepense, and holds that such a man is to be taken even from the altar — and if God will not shelter him, let him flee to the pit and let no man stay him.

Clarke explains the need for the refuge historically, since the nearest kinsman's right of vengeance was universally acknowledged and unregulated, so that a man who killed by accident might be cut down before any enquiry; he notes that before the cities of refuge were assigned the altar was the common asylum, says that smiting a parent argued peculiar depravity and therefore admitted no mercy, and turns the law against manstealing directly on the slave trade of his own day, holding that it condemns the receiver as well as the thief and makes no difference whether a man stole the person himself or paid a dealer to do it.

Ellicott reads the clause about God delivering a man into another's hand as covering a meeting brought about without human contrivance, presses the novelty of the provision — that throughout the East blood had been exacted for blood however sudden or excusable, and no right of asylum had ever been established before the Sinaitic law interposed the city of refuge — would render the word for presumptuously as maliciously or with premeditation, and observes that most of the ancient world scrupled to execute a man who had taken sanctuary and held those who did so accursed, a scruple the Mosaic law treated as superstition and refused to sanction. Keil and Delitzsch add that it makes no difference whether death followed on the spot or shortly after, and explain the accidental case of a man who intended not merely no killing but no harm, so that what happened was by a dispensation of God which we call accident only because it is above our comprehension.

debates: Whether accidental homicide is chance or providence. Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin both refer it to the will of God, Calvin adding that He led the man who is killed out to his death, and Keil and Delitzsch that we call it accident only because it is above our comprehension.

How the right of sanctuary stands. Clarke notes that the altar served as asylum before the cities of refuge existed; Ellicott holds that the Mosaic law deliberately refused the ancient scruple against executing a man who had reached sanctuary, treating it as superstition.

How far the law against smiting a parent extends. Gill requires a visible wound or mark but not death; Clarke rests on the peculiar depravity of the act; Calvin denies that it takes in every offence against a parent while insisting it goes beyond Roman law by punishing violence short of killing.
outliers: Ellicott's claim that no right of asylum is known to have existed anywhere before the Sinaitic legislation established the city of refuge.
Gill's list of those whose killing does not fall under the law — the court officer, the executioner, the physician, the father chastising a child.
Clarke's application of the manstealing law to the slave trade of his own day, condemning the purchaser equally with the thief.
themes: blood required for blood
an accident that is a dispensation
torn away from the altar
the rights of parents made sacred

18.pericope_label: Injuries: the quarrel, the slave, the pregnant woman, and like for like

schools.summary: Gill restricts the case of the beaten servant to a Gentile struck with a rod rather than a killing weapon, and on the law of retaliation observes that the heathen took theirs from it while reporting the division between Josephus, who understood it literally, and the Jewish writers generally, who took it for a money payment reckoned as a servant is priced in the market. Calvin thinks the penalty for wounds too slight and warns from Roman experience what a light fine invites, holds that God has no respect of persons in the matter of murder and avenges a slave's death as a free man's, calls it gross barbarism to have given masters the power of life and death, and refuses to limit the word for mischief to the mother, since the unborn child is already a human being and to rob it of life is almost a monstrous crime.

Henry dwells on the tenderness of the provision for a pregnant woman, the law of nature itself forbidding that the tree and the fruit be destroyed together, and draws the comfort that women under the special protection of God's law may believe themselves under the special protection of his providence.

Clarke states the principle behind the proviso about surviving a day or two — that the death might then be presumed to have another cause, all penal laws being construed as favourably as possible to the accused — and explains the weight of the offence against a pregnant woman by the place of posterity in the covenant, every man hoping the Messiah might spring from his family, noting that the fine lay with the husband though a fatal outcome was punished as in other cases. Wesley restricts the case to a Gentile servant struck with a rod rather than a mortal weapon, and leaves the punishment to the discretion of the judges upon the circumstances.

Ellicott holds that a charge of murder was not to hang over a man indefinitely, so that once the injured party was about again the offender was quit whatever followed, marks the protection of the slave's life as unprecedented since hitherto a slave had been absolutely his master's property and notes that the Talmud made the master liable to death, supports the presumption of unintended killing by the pecuniary loss a master inflicted on himself, supposes the hurt to a pregnant woman accidental and arising from her interference in her husband's quarrel, and reads the qualifying clause as meaning nothing beyond the loss of the child. Keil and Delitzsch set out the rule of compensation for lost time and cure and infer that death on the bed would have fallen under the law of murder, note that the right of chastisement was never in question but only its abuse, and limit the law of like for like to the free Israelite, the slave's master forfeiting him altogether for an eye or a tooth.

debates: Whether the law of retaliation was literal or pecuniary. Gill reports Josephus for the literal sense and the Jewish writers generally for a money payment priced as a servant is priced; Keil and Delitzsch bypass the question and fix instead on its not applying to slaves at all.

What the clause about mischief covers. Ellicott takes it to mean nothing beyond the loss of the child, so that the fine alone applies; Calvin refuses to confine the word to the mother, since the unborn child is already a human being and killing it would otherwise go uncapital.
Whether the penalties are severe enough. Calvin objects that a slight penalty for wounds may provoke the ill-disposed, citing the Roman fine that was mocked into disuse.
outliers: Calvin's story of the Roman who boxed the ears of passers-by while a slave followed him paying the statutory fine.
Ellicott's claim that the protection of a slave's life here is the first known in any code.
Ellicott's second reason for presuming a killing unintended, that the master destroyed his own property.
themes: liability that ends when a man walks again
a slave's life brought under the law
the child in the womb already a man
eye for eye, or the price of an eye

28.pericope_label: The goring ox and the uncovered pit

schools.summary: Gill refuses to confine the protection to Israelites, since a man of another nation gored by an Israelite's ox brought the same penalty, reports the rabbinic definition of a beast with a habit as one that had pushed three days before, notes that the commutation supposes carelessness rather than ill design and requires the family's consent, takes the clause about a son or daughter of children as against grown persons and repeats that every life is equally guarded, doubts the rabbinic confinement of the slave's case to a Canaanite, and describes the pit as either an old one uncovered or a new one dug in a public place. Calvin meets the objection that punishing a brute is childish, since oxen were created for man's good and their death may serve him as their life did, inclines to read the clause about a son as making a father liable for his own child's death by his own ox while admitting the hardness of it, defends the thirty shekels on the ground that mischance may be treated more mildly than voluntary murder when the stoning of the ox already brings bloodshed into detestation, and holds that such carelessness approaches actual guilt though the payer may keep the carcass since there was no fraud.

Clarke thinks a bull rather than an ox is meant, notes that most nations legislated against the danger and that the Romans twisted hay about a dangerous beast's horns as a warning, states that the forfeited life might be commuted for a payment at which the magistrates valued the deceased, converts the thirty shekels into English money to reckon a slave's life at something over four pounds and observes that this was the price at which the same people afterwards valued the life of Christ, restricts the pit to a public place since a man might do as he pleased in his own ground, and suspects that two of these verses stand out of their proper order.

Ellicott explains the stoning as the death of a murderer and the prohibition of the flesh by the fact that a beast so killed would not be bled and would be unclean, adds that the rabbis required the carcass to be buried rather than sold to Gentiles, marking any creature that had taken human life as accursed, holds it clear that the family might have exacted life for life while thinking they would almost always have taken compensation, notes that the ransom was laid primarily by the aggrieved relatives with an appeal to the judges if exorbitant, and would render the pit clause as uncovering a well, since eastern wells have covers lifted for drawing and then replaced. Keil and Delitzsch mark the transition from life to property, the working animal being the Israelite's most important possession and now secured against destruction by carelessness.

debates: What the clause about a son or a daughter means. Gill takes it of children as against adults, extending the same protection to little ones; Calvin leaves the question of age open but inclines to make it a father's liability for his own child killed by his own ox.

How the thirty shekels should be judged. Calvin defends the sum as a proper mitigation where the death came by mischance and the ox had already been made the example; Clarke reduces it to English money to show how little a slave's life was reckoned, and turns the figure on the later valuation of Christ.
What the pit clause covers. Gill and Clarke read it of opening an old pit or digging a new one in a public place; Ellicott would render it more exactly as failing to replace the cover of a well.
outliers: Clarke's Roman parallel of hay twisted about a dangerous beast's horns, and the proverb that followed from it.
Ellicott's report that the rabbis would not let the carcass be sold even to Gentiles, but required it to be buried.
Calvin's concession that it might seem hard to condemn a father already weighed down by the loss of his child.
themes: a beast that dies a murderer's death
a life forfeit and a life ransomed
thirty shekels for a servant
the well left uncovered
